title: Airport Security: New Scanners, Liquid Rules and How to Get Through Faster
metaDescription: What has changed at airport security — CT scanners, the 100ml liquid rule, trusted traveller programmes — and the habits that get you through the queue quickly.
excerpt: Security rules are changing unevenly across airports, which means the only safe assumption is the strictest one.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
Airport security is in an awkward transition. New scanner technology at some airports removes the need to take out liquids and laptops entirely; at the airport next door, the old rules apply in full. Some airports have relaxed the 100ml limit and then reinstated it.

The result is that the only workable approach is to **pack for the strictest rule** and be pleasantly surprised when it does not apply.

## What Changed: CT Scanners

The new generation of computed tomography scanners produces a 3D image that security staff can rotate and inspect, which means bags no longer need to be decanted. At airports fully equipped with them, you typically leave laptops, tablets and liquids **inside your bag**, and in some cases the 100ml limit is relaxed.

The complications are real:

- **Rollout is uneven.** Major hubs have them; many airports do not, and some have them in only a few lanes.
- **Rules have been reinstated.** Several airports that relaxed liquid limits later reverted, sometimes at short notice, for operational and regulatory reasons.
- **Your outbound and return airports may differ.** You can fly out of an airport that lets you keep a full water bottle and return through one that does not.

**The practical rule: pack liquids to the 100ml standard regardless.** If the scanner is modern, you have lost nothing. If it is not, you have not lost your toiletries.

## The 100ml Rule, Precisely

Where it applies — which is still most places:

- Containers of **100ml or less each**, by the container's stated capacity, not by how full it is. A half-empty 200ml bottle is not permitted
- All containers fitting comfortably in **one transparent resealable bag of roughly one litre**
- **One bag per passenger**
- Removed from your luggage and placed separately in a tray, unless the airport says otherwise

What counts as a liquid catches people out: gels, pastes, creams, aerosols, mascara, lip balm, and anything with a soft or spreadable consistency. Yoghurt and soft cheese count. Peanut butter counts.

**Exemptions**, which generally do apply:

- **Medication**, in reasonable quantity, ideally in original packaging with a prescription or doctor's letter
- **Baby food, formula and milk** for an infant travelling with you
- Both are usually screened separately, so declare them rather than hiding them in the bag

![Airports travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1709144281357-83b30491c0a0?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## What Cannot Go in Hand Luggage

Beyond liquids:

- **Sharp objects** — scissors above a small blade length, razor blades, knives of any kind, multi-tools
- **Sporting goods** that could be used as a weapon
- **Flammables** — lighter fluid, camping gas, certain aerosols

And, critically, some things cannot go in **checked** luggage:

- **Lithium batteries and power banks must be in hand luggage**, never in the hold. This is a fire-safety rule and it is enforced. Power banks above a certain capacity may be restricted entirely, and some airlines have added rules about using or charging them in flight
- **Spare batteries** of any kind
- **E-cigarettes and vapes** must be carried in the cabin and generally not used or charged on board

The most common delay at security is a power bank at the bottom of a checked bag that has to be retrieved.

## Getting Through Faster

The queue is mostly other people's disorganisation. Some of it is yours, and that part is fixable.

**Before you leave home**
- Pack the liquids bag **at the top** of your carry-on, or in an outside pocket
- Put laptops and tablets somewhere you can reach in one movement
- Empty your water bottle — but bring it, because most airports have refill points after security
- Check your bag for the things that accumulate: a pocket knife, a full bottle of water, a forgotten lighter

**In the queue**
- **Empty your pockets into your bag**, not into a tray. Fewer trays, fewer things to forget, faster on the other side
- Take off your belt, watch and heavy jacket **before** you reach the front
- Shoes: depends on the airport and increasingly not required, but be ready
- Have your boarding pass and passport out and in hand

**After the scanner**
- Move your trays to the reclaim bench and repack there, not at the belt. This is the single most useful piece of queue etiquette and almost nobody does it

**Choosing a lane**
- Avoid lanes with families and large groups — not unkindness, just arithmetic
- Lanes at the far ends are usually shorter than the ones directly ahead of the entrance
- If there is a dedicated lane for hand luggage only, it is almost always faster

![Airports travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1560580184-2f022cabec4a?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Trusted Traveller Programmes

If you fly more than a few times a year, these pay for themselves in time.

- **TSA PreCheck** (US domestic) — no shoes, belt or laptop removal, shorter queues
- **Global Entry** (US) — expedited US immigration on arrival, and includes PreCheck. The queue for an interview appointment can be long, so apply well ahead
- **Registered Traveller schemes** in the UK and Europe — vary by country, generally expedite immigration rather than security
- **Airport-specific fast-track** — purchasable per trip at many airports, and worth it on a tight connection or at a notoriously slow airport
- **Airline status and premium cabins** usually include fast-track access

For immigration rather than security, **automated e-gates** are increasingly open to a wider set of nationalities and are dramatically faster than a staffed desk. Check eligibility before queuing for a booth.

## How Early Should You Arrive?

Airline guidance is deliberately conservative. Realistic minimums, assuming hand luggage only and a normal day:

- **Domestic, small airport** — 60 minutes
- **Domestic, major hub** — 75–90 minutes
- **International** — 2 hours
- **International at a very busy hub, or in peak season** — 2.5 to 3 hours
- **Anywhere during a major holiday period** — add an hour to all of the above

Add 30 minutes if you are checking a bag, and check the specific airport's reputation. A few well-known airports have security queues that regularly run far beyond the norm, and locals plan around them.

## The Connection Trap

The mistake that ruins trips: booking a short connection at an airport where you have to **clear security or immigration again**.

This happens more often than people expect — changing between terminals, arriving from outside a customs union, or transferring between separate tickets. A 50-minute connection is fine airside within one terminal and impossible if you have to re-enter through security.

Check the minimum connection time for the specific airport, and if the two flights are on separate tickets, allow several hours rather than the minimum. The airline owes you nothing when a separate ticket goes wrong.

## Families and Accessibility

- **Families with young children** can usually use priority or family lanes. Ask
- **Pushchairs** go through the scanner or are gate-checked
- **Assistance** must be requested in advance, usually at least 48 hours, through the airline. It is free and it significantly improves the experience
- **Medical devices, prosthetics and implants** — tell the officer before screening. A doctor's letter helps but is not usually required

When travelling with a group, the security queue is where everyone separates and nobody has agreed a meeting point. Two minutes of planning — "we regroup at the gate, not after security" — saves the twenty minutes of milling that otherwise follows. Small enough to feel unnecessary, and exactly the sort of thing worth writing into the shared plan alongside the flight details.
